newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan heavyweights in final race for votes.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan heavyweights in final race for votes.

text.p: Ousted Pakistan prime minister Benazir Bhutto and her main opponent started their final bid for votes on Friday amid strong signs of deep public apathy for the country's fifth election in 12 years.
Bhutto and former prime minister Nawaz Sharif, widely seen as the likely winner of Monday's elections, were concentrating their energies on Punjab, Pakistan's most populous province.
Both set off to criss-cross Punjab before hitting Lahore, the provincial capital, on Sunday for a series of mass rallies.

So far, their rallies have been relatively poorly attended and political analysts say the electorate appears fed up with Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) and Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League (PML), both widely accused of corruption.
Some newspaper pundits have predicted a voter turnout as low as 20 percent -- compared with 69 percent in 1988 and 40 percent in 1993.

But they say campaign apathy may have also stemmed from uncertainty about whether the polls would go ahead. Bhutto had appealed to the Supreme Court against her sacking on November 5 by President Farooq Leghari on disputed corruption charges.
Wednesday's decision by the court to uphold Leghari's action removed that uncertainty, to the delight of stock markets which jumped in anticipation of a pro-business Sharif government.

Newspaper editorials appealed on Friday for the bitterness over the court case to be put aside and called for a credible poll in a country where the stock of politicians has nose-dived and the economy is in a wretched state.

"Our first priority should now be to ensure that the elections take place in a free, fair and transparent manner," said The News, predicting that the tempo of an unprecedentedly dull campaign should now pick up.
"The world will be watching and we cannot afford to have them laughing at us," the English-language daily added.
Sharif's PML is widely predicted to emerge as the largest party in the 217-seat National Assembly, the lower house of parliament, but short of an overall majority.
The latest opinion poll, by Gallup Pakistan and published earlier this week, predicted the PML would win around 40 percent of the vote nationwide against some 20 percent for the PPP.
It did, however, say Bhutto's party usually added five to 10 percentage points in the last few days before elections.

The Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement), led by former Pakistani cricket captain Imran Khan, a national hero and a new entrant into the country's political stakes, is seen as unlikely to make a significant impact.
Political analysts say the party is too new, bereft of a nationwide organisation and its candidates are too unknown to make a serious dent in traditional voting patterns.

They say the role of king-maker, should the PML not win an overall majority, could fall to the ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM), which expects to win around a dozen seats in Karachi and other cities in the southern province of Sindh.

The MQM, which represents Moslems who crossed from India to Pakistan when India was partitioned at independence in 1947, is bitterly opposed to Bhutto, whose main strongholds lie in the rural interior of Sindh.
The MQM blames her for thousands of deaths in Karachi, the provincial capital, in a crackdown on MQM militants.
